missions/ecumenical-mission/name: Edinburgh 1910, the International Missionary Council and the World Council of Churches
missions/ecumenical-mission/statusNote: The International Missionary Council was integrated into the World Council of Churches in 1961 as the Commission on World Mission and Evangelism, which still holds world mission conferences (Arusha 2018). The ecumenical missionary movement was transformed from a Western Protestant missionary alliance into a fellowship of churches, most of whose members are now in the global South, with much less emphasis on sending missionaries.
missions/ecumenical-mission/summary: The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in June 1910, chaired by John R. Mott and organised by J. H. Oldham, sought to coordinate Protestant missions for ‘the evangelization of the world in this generation’. Its Continuation Committee became the International Missionary Council (1921), whose conferences at Jerusalem (1928), Tambaram (1938), Whitby (1947) and Willingen (1952) reshaped thinking on the indigenous church and the missio Dei. Merged into the World Council of Churches in 1961, the ecumenical stream broadened mission to include justice, dialogue and humanisation — a turn that provoked the evangelical–ecumenical split.
missions/ecumenical-mission/story:
The World Missionary Conference met in the Assembly Hall of the United Free Church of Scotland in Edinburgh from 14 to 23 June 1910. Its 1,215 official delegates represented Protestant missionary societies — Anglican, Reformed, Lutheran, Methodist, Baptist and others — overwhelmingly from Britain, North America and continental Europe; fewer than twenty came from Asia and almost none from Africa. Roman Catholic and Orthodox missions were not represented, and to secure Anglo-Catholic participation the organisers excluded Latin America and other ‘Christian’ lands from the survey of fields. The eight commission reports surveyed the non-Christian world, the church on the mission field, education, other religions, missionary preparation, home base, government relations and cooperation. The most remembered speech was V. S. Azariah’s plea for genuine partnership: ‘You have given your goods to feed the poor. You have given your bodies to be burned. We also ask for love. Give us friends!’

Edinburgh’s Continuation Committee, with Mott as chair and Oldham as secretary, launched the International Review of Missions (1912), sponsored Mott’s 1912–13 tour of national conferences across Asia that led to national Christian councils, and survived the First World War, which shattered the confidence and internationalism of 1910 and saw German missions expelled from British territories. The International Missionary Council was formed at Lake Mohonk, New York, in 1921. At Jerusalem in 1928 it confronted secularism and the relationship between Christianity and other religions; the American Laymen’s Foreign Missions Inquiry (Re-Thinking Missions, 1932, chaired by W. E. Hocking) proposed that missions should seek common ground with other faiths and emphasise social service, provoking conservative outrage. At Tambaram, near Madras, in 1938 — the first conference at which delegates from the ‘younger churches’ were a majority — Hendrik Kraemer’s The Christian Message in a Non-Christian World argued for a ‘biblical realism’ discontinuous with other religions, against Indian theologians such as P. Chenchiah who sought continuity.

After 1945 the IMC reckoned with decolonisation. Whitby (1947) spoke of ‘partnership in obedience’ between older and younger churches. The expulsion of missionaries from China after 1949 forced a deep rethink, and at Willingen (1952) the idea of the missio Dei — that mission is first God’s own activity, in which the church participates — became central. Church unions such as the Church of South India (1947) embodied the conviction that division was a scandal on the mission field. The World Council of Churches, founded in Amsterdam in 1948 from the Faith and Order and Life and Work movements, absorbed the IMC at its New Delhi assembly in 1961, where Lesslie Newbigin argued for the integration of church and mission and the Russian and other Orthodox churches joined. Some evangelical missions and national councils, wary of the WCC, distanced themselves from the integration.

The 1960s shifted the agenda. The Mexico City conference (1963) spoke of ‘mission in six continents’, ending the idea that the West was only a sender. At Uppsala (1968) the WCC’s theme, ‘Behold, I make all things new’, and its study on ‘The Missionary Structure of the Congregation’ emphasised humanisation, development and the world as the arena of God’s action; Donald McGavran asked publicly ‘Will Uppsala betray the two billion?’ The Programme to Combat Racism (1969), with grants to southern African liberation movements, divided member churches. The Bangkok conference of the Commission on World Mission and Evangelism (December 1972–January 1973), on ‘Salvation Today’, defined salvation in personal, social, economic and political dimensions and gave voice to Third World churches’ anger at Western control; Kenyan Presbyterian leader John Gatu’s call (1971) for a temporary moratorium on foreign missionaries and funds was debated there and endorsed by the All Africa Conference of Churches at Lusaka in 1974.

Evangelicals saw these developments as a betrayal of Edinburgh’s evangelistic purpose and organised separately: the Wheaton Congress on the Church’s Worldwide Mission (April 1966), the Berlin World Congress on Evangelism (October–November 1966) and the Lausanne Congress (1974). The ecumenical side, for its part, criticised evangelicals for neglecting justice and for complicity with Western power. Later ecumenical documents sought a balance: Mission and Evangelism: An Ecumenical Affirmation (1982), the conferences at Melbourne (1980, ‘Your Kingdom Come’, on the poor) and San Antonio (1989), and Together Towards Life (2012), which spoke of ‘mission from the margins’. In 2010 the centenary of Edinburgh was marked by a conference that, unlike 1910, included Catholics, Orthodox, Pentecostals and evangelicals.

Historians such as Brian Stanley regard Edinburgh 1910 as both the high-water mark of Western missionary confidence — sure that Christianity and Western civilisation would together transform the world — and the starting point of modern ecumenism. Its successors made real gains in indigenous leadership, church union and theology of mission, but the movement also lost much of its missionary-sending energy, and mainline missionary numbers fell sharply from the 1960s while evangelical and Pentecostal sending grew.
missions/ecumenical-mission/beliefs/0: Christian unity is integral to mission: divided churches undermine the credibility of the gospel (John 17:21)
missions/ecumenical-mission/beliefs/1: The missio Dei: mission belongs primarily to God, and the church participates in God’s mission in the world
missions/ecumenical-mission/beliefs/2: Mission is holistic, embracing evangelism, service, justice, peace, dialogue and care for creation
missions/ecumenical-mission/beliefs/3: Churches in every land are equal partners; mission is ‘from everywhere to everywhere’ (mission in six continents)
missions/ecumenical-mission/beliefs/4: Respectful dialogue with people of other faiths, with debate over continuity versus discontinuity (Kraemer vs fulfilment theology)
missions/ecumenical-mission/beliefs/5: Salvation includes personal, social, economic and political liberation (Bangkok 1973)
missions/ecumenical-mission/strategies/0: World conferences and study commissions producing shared reports and statements
missions/ecumenical-mission/strategies/1: National Christian councils (e.g. the National Christian Council of India, 1923) to coordinate missions and churches
missions/ecumenical-mission/strategies/2: Cooperation in education, literature, medicine and theological training (e.g. union colleges and hospitals)
missions/ecumenical-mission/strategies/3: Comity agreements dividing territories between missions to avoid competition
missions/ecumenical-mission/strategies/4: Church union schemes merging denominations founded by different missions (CSI 1947, CNI 1970)
missions/ecumenical-mission/strategies/5: Advocacy and programmes on racism, development and human rights (Programme to Combat Racism, 1969)
missions/ecumenical-mission/groupsReache: Protestant mission agencies and their ‘younger churches’ in Asia, Africa and Latin America
Orthodox churches after 1961, and Roman Catholic observers after the Second Vatican Council
Educated Christian elites and theologians of the global South who led national councils
Refugees and victims of war through inter-church aid (from 1944)
Indigenous and liberation movements supported by WCC programmes
Students through the World Student Christian Federation (1895), a key ecumenical training ground
missions/ecumenical-mission/challenges/0: Two world wars destroyed the 1910 vision of Christian civilisation and divided missionary nations
missions/ecumenical-mission/challenges/1: Decolonisation and the expulsion of missionaries from China (1949–52) forced rethinking of mission structures
missions/ecumenical-mission/challenges/2: Tension between unity and truth: conservative churches feared theological liberalism and doctrinal compromise
missions/ecumenical-mission/challenges/3: Disputes over relations with other religions and the uniqueness of Christ
missions/ecumenical-mission/challenges/4: Financial and numerical decline of the Western mainline churches that funded the movement
missions/ecumenical-mission/challenges/5: Political controversies (Programme to Combat Racism, Cold War accusations of bias) that alienated members
missions/ecumenical-mission/harms/0: Edinburgh 1910 was dominated by Western missionaries and largely shared assumptions of racial and civilisational superiority
missions/ecumenical-mission/harms/1: Exclusion of Latin America from the 1910 agenda tacitly endorsed the view that it needed no evangelisation while ignoring Protestants already there
missions/ecumenical-mission/harms/2: Critics argue the later emphasis on humanisation and political liberation marginalised evangelism and weakened missionary commitment
missions/ecumenical-mission/harms/3: Comity arrangements sometimes divided peoples arbitrarily between missions and froze denominational boundaries
missions/ecumenical-mission/harms/4: Bitter polarisation with evangelicals produced duplicated structures and mutual caricature for decades
missions/ecumenical-mission/developments: Gave churches of the global South a voice in world Christianity and promoted indigenous leadership
Produced influential missiology: missio Dei, partnership, contextualisation and holistic mission
Fostered church unions such as the Church of South India and Church of North India
Built cooperative institutions in education, health and refugee relief
Brought Orthodox, and later Catholic and Pentecostal, partners into common reflection on mission
Its emphasis on justice and dialogue shaped later evangelical thinking, including the Lausanne Covenant
missions/ecumenical-mission/outcome: The ecumenical missionary movement institutionalised cooperation and transformed mission theology, but its sending energy declined with the Western mainline churches. Its quarrel with evangelicals after 1960 created two parallel global networks, which began to converge in documents and meetings from the 1980s and at Edinburgh 2010.

missions/ecumenical-mission/countries/2/: The IMC’s Jerusalem conference addressed secularism and other religions.

missions/ecumenical-mission/journeys/0/t: Mott held some twenty regional and national conferences across Asia, which led to national missionary councils in India, China and Japan.
missions/ecumenical-mission/relations/0/: Evangelicals alarmed by Uppsala and Bangkok built their own global network through Wheaton and Berlin (1966) and Lausanne (1974).
missions/ecumenical-mission/relations/1/: SVM and the World Student Christian Federation supplied Edinburgh’s leadership and many delegates.
missions/ecumenical-mission/relations/2/: The ‘mission in six continents’ idea and the moratorium debate anticipated the shift to sending from the global South.
missions/ecumenical-mission/agreements/0: Shared Venn’s goal of self-governing, self-supporting, self-propagating churches.
missions/ecumenical-mission/agreements/1: From the 1980s both sides affirmed that evangelism and social responsibility belong together, converging in documents such as the 1982 Ecumenical Affirmation and the Cape Town Commitment (2010).
missions/ecumenical-mission/disagreement: Clashed over the priority of evangelism, the nature of salvation, dialogue with other religions and the authority of Scripture after Uppsala (1968) and Bangkok (1973).
McGavran attacked Uppsala for abandoning the ‘two billion’ unevangelised; ecumenicals criticised Church Growth’s numerical focus and the homogeneous-unit principle.
Many faith missions and their churches refused to join national councils linked to the WCC, fearing liberal theology.
missions/ecumenical-mission/deviations/0: Departed from Edinburgh 1910’s focus on evangelising the non-Christian world towards broader agendas of justice, development and dialogue
missions/ecumenical-mission/deviations/1: Abandoned the 1910 assumption of Western Christian civilisation as the model for the world
missions/ecumenical-mission/deviations/2: Moved from a missionary-society alliance to a council of churches, dissolving distinct missionary structures
